idiom_name: pattern match on the element type / PartialFunction as the visitor's declared domain
implementation_notes: Scala spells the acyclic test as pattern matching rather than accept/visit: shape match { case c: Circle => ... } narrows the element directly, and a PartialFunction[Shape, Double] is literally a visitor that declares only the element types it handles, with isDefinedAt being the failed-cast test that other languages implement with instanceof or dynamic_cast. Odersky's position is that matching beats the visitor pattern in practice because visitors get bulky and slower, and libraries that must hide their case classes expose the same idea as an external visitor or a fold (circe ships fold/Folder giving one function per JSON variant). Keep a hand-written visitor when the element representation must stay hidden, since relying on custom extractors is exactly what costs the compiler's exhaustiveness check.
pitfalls: A partial match with no default raises MatchError at runtime, so the silent skip of the acyclic form must be written deliberately as a default branch or as a logged failure - there is no middle ground.
Matching on a sealed trait gives exhaustiveness precisely because the element set is closed, so a sealed hierarchy plus match is the closed-set sibling and not the acyclic pattern.
Custom extractors make matching work on hidden representations but remove the exhaustiveness warning, which is the reason circe exposes fold/Folder instead of unapply-based matching.
